fields.narrative_intro: *An overconfident person and a gobsmacked person discuss Claude Opus 5 inside a Wikipedia edit war.*
fields.panel1:
[setup]
OVERCONFIDENT PERSON: "Someone vandalized the ARC-AGI 3 page again."
GOBSMACKED PERSON: "What did they put?"
fields.panel2:
[build]
OVERCONFIDENT PERSON: "'Claude Opus 5 scored three times the next-best model.'"
GOBSMACKED PERSON: "Classic AI hype. Reverting."
fields.panel3:
[pivot]
OVERCONFIDENT PERSON: "That's... the actual Anthropic press release."
GOBSMACKED PERSON: "At five dollars per million tokens?"
fields.panel4:
[silent reaction]
[Visual: The gobsmacked person's revert finger hovers, frozen, one millimeter above the keyboard. The overconfident person slides them the Anthropic pricing page. An ongoing edit war banner blinks overhead: 'DISPUTED: IS THIS REAL?']
fields.panel5:
[punch]
GOBSMACKED PERSON: "And it's their most aligned model ever?"
OVERCONFIDENT PERSON: "Scored 2.3 on their own audit."
fields.panel6:
[button]
[Visual: The Wikipedia article now reads 'Citation needed' on every single sentence. The gobsmacked person has added a 'Neutrality disputed' tag to the word 'Anthropic.']

narrative_summary: Two editors in a Wikipedia edit war keep trying to revert Opus 5's real benchmark numbers as vandalism, because no one can believe they're true.
rationale: Candidate 1 earns its punchline through genuine escalation — the frozen revert finger is a precise visual gag, and the button of 'Citation needed' on every sentence including the word 'Anthropic' is a earned absurdist payoff rather than a restatement. It also grounds every beat in real, specific numbers (ARC-AGI 3, $5/million tokens, 2.3 alignment score) without over-explaining them, which Candidate 3 nearly matches but undercuts with a weaker closing line.
